entities.summary:
Pedro de Alcántara Álvarez de Toledo y Salm-Salm, 13th Duke of the Infantado (1768–1841), was a preeminent Spanish grandee, military officer, and politician whose career spanned the tumultuous transition from the Ancien Régime to the liberal state in early 19th-century Spain. Born into one of Spain's most ancient and powerful noble families in Madrid on July 20, 1768, he inherited vast estates and influence, becoming a central figure during the Peninsular War (1808-1814), the subsequent Bourbon Restoration, and the initial phase of the First Carlist War. His life trajectory reflects the complex loyalties and ideological shifts among the Spanish elite as the nation grappled with foreign invasion, internal political divisions, and the emerging forces of liberalism and absolutism. 

Initially serving in the Spanish Army, the Duke of Infantado gained significant prominence during the Peninsular War, commanding forces against Napoleon's invasion. Following the Mutiny of Aranjuez in 1808, he was appointed President of the Provisional Government and later served as a member of the Supreme Central and Governing Junta of the Kingdom, playing a crucial role in organizing resistance. His military career saw him participate in key engagements, including the Battle of Uclés in 1809, and he was a vocal proponent of King Ferdinand VII's return. After the war, he held various ministerial posts, including President of the Council of Ministers (Prime Minister) in 1825, navigating the complex political landscape between absolutist factions and the burgeoning liberal movement.
